title: Academic Archive
text:
My academic work has developed across engineering, scientific computing, cryptography, electronic documents, digital signatures, identity, post-quantum cryptography, and artificial intelligence.
This archive is not intended to reproduce a curriculum vitae. It is a historical view of how research questions, projects, technological artifacts, publications, students, and collaborations have evolved and intersected over time.

title: Talks
text:
Invited talks, conference presentations, panels, tutorials, workshops, and professional presentations form an important part of my academic and technical activity.
This archive is being reconstructed from curriculum records, institutional sources, event programs, and historical material. It records presentations for which there is documentary evidence; simple event attendance and academic-service activities are maintained separately.

title: Software & Data
text:
My research has produced software, technological platforms, digital infrastructures, prototypes, reference implementations, and other artifacts. This page preserves both current work and the technological history behind it.

title: Software & Data
text:
Preservation Model
The long-term preservation strategy separates three layers:

Development — source code and active collaboration environments;
Publication — stable releases associated with papers, projects, and academic outputs;
Preservation — durable research objects with persistent metadata and, where appropriate, archival repositories and DOIs.

This structure is intended to preserve relationships such as:
project → software → release → dataset → publication → student → talk

title: Teaching
text:
Teaching Philosophy
I approach teaching as a connection between formal foundations and real computational problems. In mathematics, security, cryptography, and artificial intelligence, students should understand not only how a technique works, but also the assumptions, limitations, and consequences of using it.
Practical work, critical reading, discussion, and the construction of working prototypes complement the conceptual foundations of the courses.

title: Research
text:
My research is concerned with a broad question: how can computation be made trustworthy?
Over time, this question has connected mathematical foundations, cryptographic mechanisms, electronic documents, digital signatures, public-key infrastructures, electronic identity, post-quantum cryptography, and, more recently, artificial-intelligence agents.
The research areas below are therefore not independent topics. They form a set of related problems around digital trust: how identities, actions, documents, credentials, and computational processes can be authenticated, authorized, protected, verified, preserved, and audited.

title: Research
text:
Research Foundations

Cryptography
Cryptography provides the technical foundation for much of my research.
My work has addressed cryptographic protocols and their applications to secure electronic transactions, digital signatures, authentication, electronic documents, voting systems, public-key infrastructures, and key-management systems.
A recurring concern is not only whether a cryptographic primitive is secure in isolation, but how it behaves when incorporated into a complete system involving people, software, hardware, institutions, and long-lived information.


Finite-Field Arithmetic
Efficient arithmetic over finite fields is an important foundation for cryptographic implementations.
Current work investigates polynomial-basis arithmetic over binary extension fields, particularly the selection and structure of irreducible polynomials and the cost of modular reduction. The objective is to understand how algebraic structure influences implementation cost, including the number of logical operations and circuit depth.
This line also explores computational methods for discovering and evaluating useful families of irreducible polynomials.

title: Research
text:
Digital Trust

Digital Signatures
Digital signatures have been one of the central themes of my research for more than two decades.
The work ranges from signature mechanisms and certificate infrastructures to signature policies, long-term signatures, user-centric signing models, and the relationship between a cryptographic signature and the electronic document or act that it represents.
A persistent research question is how digital evidence can remain verifiable as algorithms, certificates, software, and trust infrastructures evolve.


Public-Key Infrastructure
Public-key infrastructures connect cryptographic mechanisms to operational trust.
My research in PKI has included certificate management, certification architectures, hardware security modules, signature policies, educational PKIs, certificate validation, and the design of trust infrastructures.
This work has included both academic research and technological development in collaboration with Brazilian digital-trust initiatives.


Electronic Identity
Electronic identity extends the trust problem beyond certificates.
Current research considers authentication, identity management, attributes, authorization, verifiable credentials, and the relationship between an identity and the digital acts performed under that identity.
One objective is to develop architectures in which identity, authentication, signatures, attributes, and authorization can be composed without unnecessarily collapsing them into a single mechanism.


Electronic Documents
Electronic documents are not merely files. They are information objects whose authenticity, integrity, confidentiality, provenance, signatures, and evidentiary value may need to survive for long periods.
Research in this area includes secure document exchange, trusted timestamps, digital signatures, long-term preservation, confidentiality, cryptographic key management, and mechanisms for maintaining verifiability despite technological change.
This research has increasingly converged with electronic identity and post-quantum cryptography.

title: Research
text:
Emerging Directions

Post-Quantum Cryptography
The transition to post-quantum cryptography is not simply the replacement of one algorithm by another.
It affects certificate formats, protocols, hardware, key management, digital signatures, identity systems, software lifecycles, interoperability, and long-term electronic evidence.
My research therefore examines post-quantum migration as a systems problem, including hybrid mechanisms, legacy-system adaptation, electronic identity, certificates, network protocols, and the preservation of digitally signed information.


Artificial Intelligence & Security
Artificial intelligence creates both new security mechanisms and new security subjects.
AI can support security analysis, document processing, classification, and interaction with complex information systems. At the same time, autonomous and semi-autonomous agents introduce questions about identity, credentials, authorization, accountability, privacy, and auditability.
A current research direction investigates how an AI agent can be identified and authorized to perform consequential digital acts on behalf of a person or organization.
This connects emerging agentic systems to long-standing security concepts such as authentication, delegation, authorization, signatures, attributes, evidence, and non-repudiation.

title: Research
text:
Current Research Questions
Several questions currently connect these research areas:

AI agent identity and authority. How should an autonomous or semi-autonomous agent be identified, authenticated, and authorized when acting for a person or organization?
Accountable digital acts. What evidence should be produced when software or an AI agent performs an action with legal, financial, administrative, or security consequences?
Post-quantum transition. How can existing PKI, identity, document, and network infrastructures migrate to post-quantum cryptography without losing interoperability or historical evidence?
Long-term electronic evidence. How can electronic documents and signatures remain verifiable when algorithms, certificates, keys, software, and trust anchors change over decades?
Efficient finite-field arithmetic. Can structured families of irreducible polynomials reduce the implementation cost of arithmetic over binary extension fields?
Composable digital identity. How should identity, authentication, attributes, signatures, representation, delegation, and authorization interact in modern digital-trust architectures?
Sovereign and domain-specific AI. How can specialized AI systems operate over sensitive institutional knowledge while maintaining control over data, provenance, access, and accountability?

title: Research
text:
Research Approach
My research combines several levels of investigation:
Foundations. Mathematical structures, cryptographic algorithms, protocols, and security models.
Architectures. PKI, identity systems, electronic-document infrastructures, key-management systems, and AI-agent trust models.
Technological artifacts. Prototypes, reference implementations, software, and experimental infrastructures used to test research ideas.
Deployment and institutions. The interaction between technology, regulation, operational processes, usability, and real trust ecosystems.
This combination is deliberate. Security mechanisms that are correct in isolation may fail when embedded in larger sociotechnical systems. Conversely, practical infrastructure problems often expose research questions that are invisible at the level of individual algorithms.

title: About
text:
I am a Full Professor in the Department of Informatics and Statistics at the Federal University of Santa Catarina (UFSC), Brazil, and have worked at the intersection of computing, cryptography, and digital trust for more than three decades.
My current research focuses on information security and cryptography, particularly digital signatures, electronic documents, public-key infrastructures, electronic identity, verifiable credentials, cryptographic key management, post-quantum cryptography, and finite-field arithmetic. More recently, I have also been investigating security, identity, authorization, and accountability for artificial-intelligence agents.
I have supervised the Laboratory for Computer Security (LabSEC) at UFSC since 2000, where research has combined theoretical questions with the design and implementation of security infrastructures and technological artifacts.

title: About
text:
Academic Formation
My academic formation began in Electrical Engineering at UFSC, where I received my bachelor’s degree in 1985. I subsequently completed a master’s degree in Electrical Engineering at UFSC in 1990, working on parametric speech coding with multi-pulse excitation.
I received my PhD in Computer Science from the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS) in 1999. My doctoral research investigated nonlinear analysis of sound patterns, with a case study involving lung sounds.
From 2005 to 2006, I was a postdoctoral researcher at George Washington University in the United States.

title: About
text:
From Engineering to Computing
My professional trajectory began in engineering and industrial automation. From 1986 to 1991, I worked at Fundação CERTI in research and development related to information systems and industrial automation, including management responsibilities in the Industrial Automation Division.
In 1990–1991, I spent a period at the Robotiker technology center in Spain working with industrial robotics and automation.
I joined the Universidade do Estado de Santa Catarina (UDESC) as a professor in 1992. There, my research already included cryptography and its applications.
In 1994, I joined UFSC as a permanent faculty member. My initial research at the Department of Informatics and Statistics was associated with computational mathematics and the Laboratory of Algebraic and Symbolic Computing.

title: About
text:
LabSEC and Digital Trust
Around the turn of the millennium, my research shifted decisively toward computer security and cryptography. Research activities at LabSEC began in 2000, followed by my supervision of the laboratory.
Early research addressed secure electronic documents, electronic voting, cryptographic protocols, digital signatures, and public-key infrastructures. These themes developed into a broader research program concerned with the technological foundations of digital trust.
Over the following decades, this work expanded to certificate lifecycle management, hardware security modules, long-term digital signatures, secure document preservation, authentication, electronic identity, and national-scale trust infrastructures.
My work has also involved collaboration with Brazilian digital-trust initiatives. I coordinated the ICP-EDU working group of the Brazilian National Research and Education Network (RNP) and have participated in activities associated with ICP-Brasil.

title: About
text:
Research Evolution
A useful way to understand my research is as a sequence of connected questions:
How can computation be made trustworthy?
That question first appeared in my work through cryptography, secure protocols, and electronic documents. It subsequently led to digital signatures and public-key infrastructures, then to electronic identity and new models for credentials and authentication.
The long-term security of these systems introduced further questions about post-quantum cryptography, cryptographic agility, efficient finite-field arithmetic, and preservation of electronic evidence.
Artificial intelligence introduces another transition. Autonomous and semi-autonomous agents raise questions that are familiar to security research but appear in a new form: Who or what is acting? Under whose authority? With which credentials? How can an action be audited, attributed, authorized, or repudiated?
These questions currently connect my earlier work on digital trust with research on AI agents and personal AI.

title: About
text:
Research and Technology
I have always considered research prototypes and technological artifacts an important complement to theoretical and academic work.
Across LabSEC projects, research has resulted in software and infrastructure related to electronic documents, digital signatures, PKI, hardware security modules, certificate management, electronic identity, post-quantum migration, and civil-registration services.
The Projects and Software & Data sections document this technological trajectory in greater detail.

title: About
text:
Students and Research Community
Supervision has been a central part of my academic work. Master’s and doctoral research conducted at LabSEC has contributed to many of the research lines represented on this site, including electronic documents, cryptographic protocols, PKI, digital signatures, identity, post-quantum cryptography, and finite-field arithmetic.
Rather than treating supervision as a separate activity, I regard students as participants in a continuing research community. The Supervision section preserves this academic genealogy.

title: About
text:
Academic Memory
This website is also intended as a long-term academic archive.
Publications alone provide an incomplete account of a research career. Projects, software, technical texts, lectures, courses, students, collaborations, and unfinished research directions often explain how ideas developed and how one line of investigation led to another.
The Academic Archive therefore connects these different kinds of records and provides a historical view of my work.
